Sonata and Rondo Forms: Practice for Chapter 25

Chapter 25 of Hutchinson’s Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom with pieces from the site’s Analysed Scores Library: the plan of sonata form and its key plan, sonatina form, sonata principle, the four structural functions, and five- and seven-part rondos.

This page goes with Chapter 25, Sonata and Rondo Forms of Robert Hutchinson’s open textbook Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom. Read each section there first. These are the biggest forms in the book, so this page is a listening-and-reading guide: it tells you what to look for, and sends you to real pieces in the site’s Analysed Scores Library, where the score plays with the experts’ Roman-numeral key labels under it. The key plans below are read from that analysis data. Bar numbers are approximate (the data puts key changes at beat positions); open the piece and listen for each change.

25.1 The plan of a sonata form

Sonata form (also called first-movement form) is the main plan of Classical and later first movements. It has three large parts and the book shows a standard layout:

Part What happens Key (major-key piece)
Exposition primary theme (PT) in the tonic, a transition that moves away, a secondary theme (ST), then often a closing theme PT in I, ST in V
Development themes fragmented and sequenced, passing through several keys unstable
Recapitulation the same material again, now with the ST brought into the tonic I throughout

Read 25.1

Many pieces have two secondary themes, or no closing theme, or a development that brings in new material. In a Classical score the exposition is repeated, and the development and recapitulation are repeated together: a two-reprise form, a descendant of balanced and rounded binary (Chapter 24). Sonatina form is a sonata form with no development section; the book’s example is the “Miniature Overture” from Tchaikovsky’s Nutcracker.

Try it with a real piece. Open Mozart’s Piano Sonata K. 545, movement 1 (the “Sonata facile”). The analysis labels its keys in this order: C major, G major, then G minor, D minor, A minor, F major, and finally C major again. Match them to the plan:

  • C major is the primary theme and transition; G major (about bar 13) is the secondary theme, in the dominant;
  • the move to G minor (about bar 29) is the start of the development, which passes through D minor and A minor;
  • the F major label (about bar 41) is the beginning of the recapitulation, and C major (about bar 51) is the point where the secondary theme arrives in the tonic.
TipWhat to notice

The recapitulation of K. 545 begins in F major (the subdominant) rather than the tonic, a famous quirk. The “home” feeling arrives only when the secondary theme returns in C. That is sonata principle (25.2): the piece is not finished until the music that was in the “wrong” key at the start is heard in the home key.

25.2 Sonata principle and the monothematic sonata

Sonata principle is Charles Rosen’s idea that the key of the second theme is a large-scale dissonance that the piece must resolve: material first stated outside the tonic is restated in the tonic. It is why a recapitulation re-writes the transition so it stays at home. In a monothematic sonata (Haydn’s favourite), the primary theme reappears in the dominant where a new secondary theme would be, so the key plan carries the drama by itself. Read 25.2

25.3 Four structural functions

Peter Temko and Peter Spencer label music by what it does, not what it is called. The same bit of a movement can be assigned a function by asking four questions:

Function Sounds like Where it is typical
Expository a stable key, clear melodies, well-formed phrases with cadences primary and secondary themes, binary and ternary pieces
Transitional moving to a new key, more active texture, often ending on a half cadence and a rest between PT and ST, retransitions
Developmental sequences, fragments of themes, many keys, irregular phrase lengths the development
Terminative emphatic back-and-forth between tonic and dominant to confirm the key closing theme, coda

Read 25.3

Practise on K. 545 above. Play it and label stretches: the first four bars (expository, a theme with a cadence); the stretch after it that leaves C (transitional: look for the chord that closes it just before the secondary theme); the section in G minor, D minor and A minor (developmental); the last bars of the exposition (terminative). The library’s Roman numerals show the V and I chords alternating in terminative music.

25.4 Rondo forms

A rondo alternates a refrain (A) with episodes (B, C). A five-part rondo is A B A C A (or A B A B A), a seven-part rondo A B A C A B A. The refrain is always in the tonic. The first episode is in a closely related key (the dominant in a major piece, the relative major, III, in a minor one); the second episode ranges more widely (the tonic minor, the submediant, the subdominant). A retransition is a passage that leads back to music already heard. Hearing the first episode first away from the tonic and later in it is another sonata principle at work. Read 25.4

Hear a five-part rondo. Beethoven’s Piano Sonata Op. 49 No. 2 ends with a Tempo di Menuetto (the library’s “movement 2”). Its key labels are G major, D major, G major, C major, G major. In the plan the refrain (A, in G) is followed by an episode in the dominant (B, at about bar 20), the refrain, a second episode in the subdominant (C, at about bar 51), and the refrain again: A B A C A. Check it: does the tune that opens the piece come back each time the key returns to G?

Another rondo to read. Mozart’s K. 545, movement 3 is a rondo too; its labels run C major, G major, C major, A minor, C major. Try to say which stretches are refrain and which are episodes, and which of the refrain’s returns is shortened. (This one is for listening; the form is not as clean as the Beethoven.)

A five-part rondo you can read bar by bar: Beethoven, Für Elise. The full-score player has it (open the score; a community score, bar numbers count the pickup as bar 1). The notes give this plan:

Bars Section What the notes show
1-24 A (refrain) the famous tune in A minor, a period (see 13.9), then a second idea in bars 11-14 (chords C, G, A minor, E) that leads back to the tune
25-40 B (episode) the melody has B♭ in it from bar 26, so it leaves A minor for F major, and it ends with a few bars on the opening notes leading back
41-62 A the refrain again, built from music already heard: bars 41-48 are bars 17-24 and bars 49-60 are bars 11-22
63-84 C (episode) slow chords instead of the running figure (bars 63-79), then an ascending run through bars 80-84 into the refrain
85-106 A the refrain once more, note for note the same as bars 41-61

That is A B A C A, the book’s five-part plan. The key names for B and C are read from the accidentals and are unverified; check them with the score and your ears. Notice what a rondo can do with a retransition: bars 37-40 and 80-84 are both short passages that lead back to the refrain.

A refrain with an unusual shape: Beethoven, Sonatina in F, Anh. 5 No. 2, Rondo. (open the score). The refrain is the first eighteen bars (see 13.9 on why it is a phrase chain), and the movement returns to its opening figure in bars 19-20 and again from bar 51. I did not map the whole movement, so it stays an item to read.

The book’s seven-part rondo: Beethoven, Pathétique Sonata, III. Open the score (the full-score player: press Play, or type a bar in the Bar box; bar numbers are the printed ones, with the short upbeat as bar 0). It has 210 bars in 2/2. The score is Craig Sapp’s Humdrum encoding of the Durand 1915 edition (see the note at the end), read bar by bar for this plan. The key names come from a key-profile count over four-bar windows, so check them with your ears and the score (unverified); the repeated bars were found by comparing the notes.

Bars Section What the notes show
1-16 A (refrain) C minor, a melody over a rolling accompaniment
17-24 transition C major for four bars, then B♭
25-56 B (first episode) B♭ major, then E♭ major from bar 37 (the relative major, as the book says), back to C minor by bar 53. The tune of bars 37-44 comes back in bars 148-155 three semitones lower (E♭ down to C), pitch for pitch
57-60 retransition leading back to the refrain; bars 58-61 are played again as bars 117-120
61-72 A the refrain again: bar 62 is bar 1, and bars 63-67 and 72 match the first statement
73-104 C (second episode) leaves C minor: A♭ major (bars 81-84 and 101-104), E♭ (85-88 and 93-100) and C minor between; A♭ is the submediant, the book’s second-episode key
105-120 retransition C major, then about twelve bars on G, the dominant
121-136 A (short) the refrain’s opening: bars 121-127 match bars 62-67 and 72, then it does not continue as before
137-157 B the first episode’s tune now in C major (the tonic, and the sonata-principle move)
158-170 retransition G major, then short sequences, back to C minor at 169
171-182 A the last refrain: bars 172-177 and 177 match bars 63-67 and 72
183-210 coda C minor, with a few C major bars, ending in C minor

That is A B A C A B A with a coda: the book’s seven-part rondo. Note how it follows sonata principle: B first stands in E♭, away from the tonic, and then in the tonic, as the second theme does in a sonata.

Sonata form you can read bar by bar: Beethoven, Moonlight Sonata, III (Presto agitato). Open the score (201 bars; the exposition’s repeat is bars 2-64, with a first ending in bar 65 and a second in bar 66, and “Skip repeats” in the player plays each bar once). It is in C♯ minor. The plan comes from the notes of Sapp’s encoding; the key regions are by key-profile count (unverified), the repeats and transpositions by comparing the notes.

Bars Part What the notes show
1-14 exposition: primary theme the arpeggio theme in C♯ minor; bar 15 is bar 1 again
15-20 transition the theme restated, then new material
21-66 exposition: secondary group, closing the key region moves to the dominant side (G♯ minor from about bar 25); bars 65 and 66 are the first and second endings
67-102 development bars 68-70 take up bars 5-7 and then it moves through several keys; no return of the primary theme until bar 103
103-116 recapitulation: primary theme bars 103-110 are bars 1-8 note for note
117-158 recapitulation: secondary group bars 117-158 follow bars 21-63 of the exposition a fifth lower: the music that stood in the dominant region now stands in the tonic
159-201 coda back to the primary theme and the tonic; bar 188 is one long bar of 13.5 beats (a free, cadenza-like run)

The fifth-lower recurrence (bars 21-63 and 117-158, checked by comparing the notes) is the sonata principle in one line of data. The exact bar where the exposition’s second theme begins is not marked here, because the pitch count can’t tell a transition from a new theme; use the score and your ears.

Where these two scores come from. Craig Stuart Sapp’s Humdrum **kern encodings of Beethoven’s piano sonatas (after the Durand 1915 edition, edited by Paul Dukas), turned into MusicXML by scripts/kern/kern2xml.py and into the player’s notation by the same checked route as the other full scores. Two small differences from the printed score: the ties in Moonlight bars 164-167 and Pathétique bars 88 and 160 (a chord with only some notes tied) are left out because the converter cannot follow them. The key names and section labels are this site’s reading, not Sapp’s.

25.5 Sonata rondo and rondo character

Sonata rondo replaces the second episode with a development: A B A development A B A. The B section appears first in the dominant and then in the tonic, as in sonata form. Rondo character means a quick, light, duple-metre movement (simple or compound) with staccato touches, and it is the usual character of a Classical finale. The book’s detailed rondo walk-through is Beethoven’s Pathétique, III (a seven-part rondo in C minor, with the first episode in E♭ major, the second in the submediant, and the first episode coming back in C major); its plan is in 25.4 above. Read 25.5

25.6 Forms in a whole sonata

The book ends with the usual movements of a Classical multimovement work (a first movement in sonata form, a slow movement in a binary, ternary or sonata plan, then a minuet and trio and a rondo or sonata-rondo finale). You can see all of these in the library: pick one Mozart or Beethoven sonata and open its movements one after another.

  • Sonata K. 545: movement 1 (sonata form), movement 2 (ternary, see Chapter 24), movement 3 (rondo).
  • Beethoven Op. 2 No. 1: movement 1 (sonata form in F minor: the labels show A♭ major in the exposition and F minor again at the recapitulation) and movement 3 (minuet and trio).
NoteFor teachers
  • Where the key plans come from: the Analysed Scores Library’s analysis data (Mozart: DCML annotators; Beethoven: BPS dataset), read in order. Bar numbers on this page are approximate and not checked against a printed score. The recapitulation-in-the-subdominant remark about K. 545 and the Op. 49 No. 2 rondo reading are from the key labels plus general knowledge of the pieces; the book does not analyse these two.
  • The book’s own pieces (Mozart K. 333 and K. 284, Haydn Hob. XVI:35, Beethoven Moonlight III and Pathétique III, Mozart’s Eine kleine Nachtmusik II) are not all in the library. Moonlight I is; Moonlight III and Pathétique III are full scores in the player (25.4), from Sapp’s kern encodings.
  • Not here: drills. Form recognition in sonata and rondo form depends on listening, and a computer cannot yet generate a sonata exposition to ask about. A Timestamp Notes outline of one movement is the cheapest way to get a class to mark its sections (Timestamp Notes).
  • The text on this page is written for the site, not copied from the book (the book is under the GNU Free Documentation License).
